sentences.zh: 冕冠 長冠 委貌冠 皮弁冠 爵弁冠 通天冠 遠湤冠 高山冠 進賢冠 法冠 武冠 建華冠 方山冠 巧士冠 卻非冠 卻敵冠 樊噲冠 術氏冠 鶡冠 幘 佩 刀 印 黃赤綬 赤綬 綠綬 紫綬 青綬 黑綬 黃綬 青紺綸 后夫人服

translations.literal: Mianguan (crown cap), changguan (long cap), weimaoguan (deferential-appearance cap), pibianguan (leather-skullcap), juebianguan (noble-skullcap), tongtianguan (pierce-heaven cap), yuanyouguan (far-roaming cap), gaoshanguan (high-mountain cap), jinxianguan (advance-the-worthy cap), faguan (law cap), wuguan (martial cap), jianhuaguan (splendid-bloom cap), fangshanguan (square-mountain cap), qiaoshiguan (ingenious-gentleman cap), quefeiguan (repel-wrong cap), quediguan (repel-enemy cap), Fan Kuai cap, Shi clan cap, heguan (pheasant cap), ze (kerchief), pei (pendants), dao (sword), yin (seal), yellow-red ribbon, red ribbon, green ribbon, purple ribbon, blue-green ribbon, black ribbon, yellow ribbon, blue-black twisted cord, and attire of the empress and consorts.
translations.idiomatic: This chapter treats the mianguan and other crown types, the ze, sword and seal regalia, the graded ribbons, and the dress of the empress and imperial consorts.

sentences.zh: 范曄、司馬彪等

translations.literal: Fan Ye, Sima Biao, and others.
translations.idiomatic: Compiled from Fan Ye, Sima Biao, and associated sources.

sentences.zh: 上古穴居而野處，衣毛而冒皮，未有制度。

translations.literal: In high antiquity people dwelt in caves and lived in the open; they clothed themselves in fur and covered their heads with hides, and there were yet no regulations.
translations.idiomatic: In earliest times people lived in caves and the wilderness, wore pelts and raw hides, and had no fixed dress code at all.

sentences.zh: 後世聖人易之以絲麻，觀翬翟之文，榮華之色，乃染帛以效之，始作五采，成以爲服。

translations.literal: Later sages replaced these with silk and hemp; observing the patterns of kingfisher and sable and the splendor of their colors, they dyed fabrics to imitate them, first devised the five hues, and completed them as garments.
translations.idiomatic: Later sages introduced silk and linen, took inspiration from the plumage of kingfishers and the sheen of costly furs, dyed cloth to match those colors, and so established the five-color system that became formal dress.

sentences.zh: 見鳥獸有冠角髯胡之製，遂作冠冕纓蕤，以爲首飾。

translations.literal: Seeing that birds and beasts had crowns, horns, whiskers, and beards by nature, they then made caps, crowns, tassels, and drooping ornaments for headgear.
translations.idiomatic: Noting how birds and beasts wore crests, horns, and beards by nature, tailors fashioned caps and crowns with hanging tassels as deliberate head ornaments.

sentences.zh: 凡十二章。

translations.literal: In all there are twelve emblems.
translations.idiomatic: The full set comprises twelve symbolic motifs.

sentences.zh: 故《易》曰：「庖犧氏之王天下也，仰觀象於天，俯觀法於地，觀鳥獸之文，與地之宜，近取諸身，遠取諸物，於是始作八卦，以通神明之德，以類萬物之情。

translations.literal: Therefore the Changes says: “When Baoxi ruled the realm, he looked up to observe images in heaven, looked down to observe patterns on earth, observed the markings of birds and beasts and the suitability of the land, drew the near from his own person and the far from things, and thereby first created the eight trigrams, to communicate the virtue of spirits and gods and to classify the conditions of the myriad things.
translations.idiomatic: The Book of Changes thus says of the sage-king Baoxi: he read the sky and the earth, studied the markings of animals and the lay of the land, took lessons from his own body and from things around him, and from this devised the eight trigrams to link human ritual with spiritual power and to give order to the myriad phenomena.

sentences.zh: 」黃帝、堯、舜垂衣裳而天下治，蓋取諸乾巛。

translations.literal: ”The Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun let their upper and lower garments hang down and the realm was well governed; this is thought to have been taken from Qian and Kun.
translations.idiomatic: The Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun are said to have “let robe and skirt fall straight,” and good government followed—an image drawn, tradition holds, from the trigrams Qian and Kun.

sentences.zh: 乾巛有文，故上衣玄，下裳黃。

translations.literal: Qian and Kun have their patterns; therefore the upper garment is black and the lower skirt is yellow.
translations.idiomatic: Because Qian and Kun embody distinct patterns, ritual dress paired a black upper robe with a yellow lower skirt.

sentences.zh: 日月星辰，山龍華蟲，作繢宗彝，藻火粉米，黼黻絺繡，以五采章施於五色作服。

translations.literal: Sun, moon, and stars; mountains, dragons, and splendid insects; the ancestral urn as embroidery; water-weed, fire, powdered grain, and rice; axe-figures and opposing “fu” motifs in fine embroidery—the five colors were applied in five hues to make the robes.
translations.idiomatic: The twelve emblems—sun, moon, constellations, mountains, dragons, and the rest, down to the paired axe motifs—were woven in the five prescribed colors into the imperial vestments.

sentences.zh: 天子備章，公自山以下，侯伯自華蟲以下，子男自藻火以下，卿大夫自粉米以下。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven had the full set of emblems; dukes from the mountains downward; marquises and earls from the splendid insect downward; viscounts and barons from water-weed and fire downward; ministers and grandees from powdered grain downward.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor wore all twelve motifs; high nobility stepped down by rank—dukes kept the mountain and below, marquises the “splendid insect” and below, and so on until ministers were limited to the humbler symbols.

sentences.zh: 至周而變之，以三辰爲旂旗。

translations.literal: By the Zhou they altered this, using the three luminaries for banners and flags.
translations.idiomatic: The Zhou revised the scheme, reserving sun, moon, and stars chiefly for flags rather than the robe itself.

sentences.zh: 王祭上帝，則大裘而冕；

translations.literal: When the king sacrificed to High God, he wore the great fur robe and the mianguan;
translations.idiomatic: For the supreme sacrifice to Heaven the king donned the heavy fur outer robe and the jeweled mianguan.

sentences.zh: 公侯卿大夫之服用九章以下。

translations.literal: The robes of dukes, marquises, and ministers and grandees used nine emblems or fewer.
translations.idiomatic: Nobles and senior officials were limited to nine emblems or fewer on their court dress.

sentences.zh: 秦以戰國即天子位，滅去禮學，郊祀之服皆以袀玄。

translations.literal: Qin, having taken the throne amid the Warring States, abolished ritual learning, and for suburban sacrifices the garments were all plain black.
translations.idiomatic: The Qin founders, rising from military conquest, discarded classical ritual; even suburban sacrifices were performed in undecorated black.

sentences.zh: 漢承秦故。

translations.literal: Han inherited Qin practice.
translations.idiomatic: The Han at first continued the austere Qin wardrobe.

sentences.zh: 至世祖踐祚，都於土中，始修三雍，正兆七郊。

translations.literal: When the Founding Emperor ascended the throne and made his capital in the central plain, he began to repair the three Yong ritual complexes and to align the seven suburban altars.
translations.idiomatic: Only when Guangwu took the throne and fixed his capital at Luoyang did the court revive the three ritual enclosures and set the seven directional suburban shrines in order.

sentences.zh: 顯宗遂就大業，初服旒冕，衣裳文章，赤舄絇屨，以祠天地，養三老五更於三雍，於時致治平矣。

translations.literal: The Manifest Emperor then completed the great enterprise: he first wore the flowing tassels and mianguan, patterned robe and skirt, red shoes with braided trim, to sacrifice to Heaven and Earth and to nurture the Three Elders and Five Exemplars in the three Yong; at that time good order was achieved.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ming finished what his father had begun: he appeared in full mianguan with hanging pearls, brocade upper and lower garments, and crimson ritual shoes, to worship Heaven and Earth and to host the aged worthies at the three Yong—by then the dress code matched the peace of the age.

sentences.zh: 天子、三公、九卿、特進侯、侍祠侯，祀天地明堂，皆冠旒冕，衣裳玄上纁下。

translations.literal: The Son of Heaven, the Three Dukes, the Nine Ministers, specially advanced marquises, and marquises who attend sacrifice, when sacrificing to Heaven and Earth or in the Bright Hall, all wear the mianguan with hanging pearls, black upper garments and light-red lower skirts.
translations.idiomatic: For the great sacrifices to Heaven, Earth, and the Bright Hall, the emperor, the three highest ministers, the nine senior officials, and certain enfeoffed nobles all wore the tasseled crown with black bodice and cinnabar skirt.

sentences.zh: 乘輿備文，日月星辰十二章，三公、諸侯用山龍九章，九卿以下用華蟲七章，皆備五采，大佩，赤舄絇履，以承大祭。

translations.literal: The imperial equipage has the full pattern: sun, moon, and stars—twelve emblems; the Three Dukes and nobles use mountains and dragons—nine emblems; ministers from the Nine Ministers downward use the splendid insect—seven emblems; all have the five colors, great pendants, red shoes and braided shoes, to undertake the great sacrifices.
translations.idiomatic: The imperial carriage robe bore all twelve emblems; dukes and feudal lords stopped at nine; the nine ministers and below used seven—all in the five prescribed colors, with the great jade girdle-pendants and crimson court shoes for the highest rites.

sentences.zh: 百官執事者，冠長冠，皆祗服。

translations.literal: The hundred officials who carry out the duties wear the changguan and all wear reverent dress.
translations.idiomatic: Rank-and-file ritual officers wore the tall “long cap” and the plain black vestments appointed for their tasks.

sentences.zh: 五嶽、四瀆、山川、宗廟、社稷諸沾秩祠，皆袀玄長冠，五郊各如方色云。

translations.literal: For the Five Marchmounts, Four Streams, mountains and rivers, ancestral temples, altars of soil and grain, and all the ranked shrines that receive regular offerings, all wear plain black changguan; the five suburban sacrifices each follow the color of its quarter.
translations.idiomatic: For the great mountains, rivers, lineage shrines, and soil-and-grain altars, officers wore the black changguan, while each of the five directional suburban rites used the color of its compass sector.

sentences.zh: 百官不執事，各服常冠袀玄以從。

translations.literal: The hundred officials who are not carrying out duties each wear their ordinary cap and plain black to follow along.
translations.idiomatic: Officials not directly officiating simply put on everyday caps and black dress to join the procession.

sentences.zh: 冕冠，垂旒，前後邃延，玉藻。

translations.literal: The mianguan: hanging pearls, front and rear deep extensions, jade ornaments on the tassels.
translations.idiomatic: The state crown was the mianguan—front and rear veils of pearls, with jade beads strung on the hanging threads.

sentences.zh: 孝明皇帝永平二年，初詔有司採《周官》、《禮記》、《尚書·皋陶篇》，乘輿服從歐陽氏說，公卿以下從大小夏侯氏說。

translations.literal: In the second year of Yongping of Emperor Xiaoming, he first ordered the authorities to draw on the Offices of Zhou, the Record of Rites, and the “Gao Yao” chapter of the Documents: the imperial equipage followed the Ou-yang school, while dukes and ministers downward followed the Greater and Lesser Xiahou schools.
translations.idiomatic: In 59 CE Emperor Ming directed the ministry to harmonize the Rites of Zhou, the Book of Rites, and the “Gao Yao” text: the emperor’s regalia followed the Ou-yang interpretation, while that of the bureaucracy followed the two Xiahou traditions.

sentences.zh: 冕皆廣七寸，長尺二寸，前圓後方，朱綠裏，玄上，前垂四寸，後垂三寸，系白玉珠爲十二旒，以其綬採色爲組纓。

translations.literal: All mianguan are seven inches wide and one foot two inches long, round in front and square behind, with vermilion-green lining and black on top; the front hangs four inches and the rear three; white jade beads form twelve tassels, and the cord and tassel colors follow the ribbon’s hues.
translations.idiomatic: The standard mianguan measured seven inches by a foot two, round toward the audience and square at the back, lined in red-green and covered in black silk, with twelve white-jade strings of pearls whose tie-colors matched the wearer’s ribbon.

sentences.zh: 三公諸侯七旒，青玉爲珠；

translations.literal: The Three Dukes and nobles have seven tassels, with green jade for beads;
translations.idiomatic: Dukes and enfeoffed lords were limited to seven pearl strings of green jade.

sentences.zh: 卿大夫五旒，黑玉爲珠。

translations.literal: ministers and grandees have five tassels, with black jade for beads.
translations.idiomatic: Senior ministers wore five strings, threaded with black jade.

sentences.zh: 皆有前無後，各以其綬採色爲組纓，旁垂黈纊。

translations.literal: All have front tassels but none behind; each uses his ribbon’s color for the cord and tassel, with yellow tassel-wads hanging at the side.
translations.idiomatic: These crowns had veils only in front; cords and tassels matched each man’s ribbon, with yellow silk wads at the temples.

sentences.zh: 郊天地，宗祀，明堂，則冠之。

translations.literal: For suburban sacrifice to Heaven and Earth, for lineage sacrifice, and for the Bright Hall, they wear it.
translations.idiomatic: It was reserved for the greatest state sacrifices—to Heaven and Earth, the imperial ancestors, and inside the Bright Hall.

sentences.zh: 衣裳玉佩備章採，乘輿刺繡，公侯九卿以下皆織成，陳留襄邑獻之云。

translations.literal: Robe and skirt, jade pendants, and full emblem colors are complete; the imperial equipage is embroidered, while dukes, marquises, and ministers downward all have woven fabric, presented, it is said, from Xiangyi in Chenliu.
translations.idiomatic: Court dress displayed the full set of emblems and jade girdle ornaments: the emperor’s was embroidered, while nobles and officials wore loom-woven brocade said to have been sent up each year from Xiangyi.

sentences.zh: 長冠，一曰齋冠，高七寸，廣三寸，促漆纚爲之，制如板，以竹爲裡。

translations.literal: The changguan, also called the fasting cap, is seven inches high and three inches wide, made of tight-wrapped lacquered gauze, shaped like a board, with bamboo inside.
translations.idiomatic: The “long cap,” also named the fasting cap, stood seven inches high, was stiffened with lacquered mesh over a bamboo frame, and looked like a narrow board on the head.

sentences.zh: 初，高祖微時，以竹皮爲之，謂之劉氏冠，楚冠制也。

translations.literal: At first, when Gaozu was still obscure, he made it from bamboo skin and called it the Liu clan cap, in the Chu cap style.
translations.idiomatic: When Liu Bang was still a commoner he fashioned such a cap from bamboo bark—the “Liu family cap,” modeled on southern Chu headgear.

sentences.zh: 民謂之鵲尾冠，非也。

translations.literal: The common people call it the magpie-tail cap; this is incorrect.
translations.idiomatic: Folk nicknamed it the “magpie-tail cap,” but that name is a mistake.

sentences.zh: 祀宗廟諸祀則冠之。

translations.literal: For sacrifice in the ancestral temple and the various sacrifices they wear it.
translations.idiomatic: It was prescribed for ancestral rites and other major temple sacrifices.

sentences.zh: 皆服袀玄，絳緣領袖爲中衣，絳褲襪，示其赤心奉神也。

translations.literal: All wear plain black, with crimson borders on collar and cuffs for the inner garment, crimson trousers and socks, showing their red hearts in serving the spirits.
translations.idiomatic: Wearers paired it with plain black robes, crimson-trimmed underlayers, and red legwear—symbolizing an undivided heart turned toward the gods.

sentences.zh: 五郊，衣幘褲襪各如其色。

translations.literal: For the five suburban sacrifices, cap, kerchief, trousers, and socks each follow that quarter’s color.
translations.idiomatic: At the five directional suburban altars, kerchief, leggings, and socks matched the color of the rite’s compass direction.

sentences.zh: 此冠高祖所造，故以爲祭服，尊敬之至也。

translations.literal: This cap was created by Gaozu, and therefore is taken as sacrificial dress, the utmost in reverence.
translations.idiomatic: Because the founder himself had devised it, the court treated this cap as the most solemn possible ritual headgear.

sentences.zh: 委貌冠、皮弁冠同制，長七寸，高四寸，制如覆杯，前高廣，後卑銳，所謂夏之毋追，殷之章甫者也。

translations.literal: The weimaoguan and pibianguan share one pattern, seven inches long and four inches high, shaped like an inverted cup, high and broad in front, low and pointed behind—what are called the Xia “Wu zhui” and the Shang “Zhang fu.”
translations.idiomatic: The deferential cap and the leather crown shared one silhouette—like an upside-down bowl, higher in front—corresponding to antiquity’s Wu zhui of the Xia and Zhang fu of the Shang.

sentences.zh: 委貌以皁絹爲之，皮弁以鹿皮爲之。

translations.literal: The weimao is made of black silk gauze, the pibian of deerskin.
translations.idiomatic: Court tailors built the deferential cap from black gauze and the bian cap from tanned deerhide.

sentences.zh: 行大射禮於辟雍，公卿諸侯大夫行禮者，冠委貌，衣玄端素裳。

translations.literal: When performing the great archery rite in the Yong, dukes, marquises, earls, and grandees who take part in the ritual wear the weimao, black upper robe, and plain lower skirt.
translations.idiomatic: At the great archery ceremony in the ritual park, participating nobles wore the deferential cap with a black “duan” jacket and undyed skirt.

sentences.zh: 執事者冠皮弁，衣緇麻衣，皁領袖，下素裳，所謂皮弁素積者也。

translations.literal: Those who carry out the duties wear the pibian, black hemp coat, black collar and cuffs, plain lower skirt below—what is called “pibian with plain pleated skirt.”
translations.idiomatic: Officiants instead donned the leather crown, ink-dyed hemp coat with black facings, and white pleated skirt—the combination classic texts call “leather crown, plain accumulation.”

sentences.zh: 爵弁，一名冕。

translations.literal: The juebian, another name is mianguan.
translations.idiomatic: The “noble skullcap” (juebian) was sometimes classed among the mianguan family.

sentences.zh: 廣八寸，長尺二寸，如爵形，前小後大，繒其上似爵頭色，有收持笄，所謂夏收殷{曰籲}者也。

translations.literal: Eight inches wide, one foot two inches long, shaped like a jue-vessel, small in front and large in back; silk on top in the color of a jue’s lip; it has a pin to secure it—what are called the Xia shou and Yin xu styles.
translations.idiomatic: It measured eight by twelve inches, flared like a bronze jue, dyed on the crown to suggest a cup’s rim, and fastened with a hairpin—the forms antiquity knew as the Xia shou and Shang xu caps.

sentences.zh: 祠天地五郊明堂，《雲翹舞》樂人服之。

translations.literal: For sacrifice to Heaven and Earth at the five suburbs and in the Bright Hall, the musicians of the “Cloud-Rising” dance wear it.
translations.idiomatic: Dancers in the “Cloud Ascent” performance wore it for Heaven, Earth, the five directional rites, and the Bright Hall.

sentences.zh: 《禮》曰：「朱幹玉鏚，冕而舞《大夏》。

translations.literal: The Record of Rites says: “Vermilion shield and jade axe—crowned thus they dance the Great Xia.”
translations.idiomatic: The Book of Rites describes dancers bearing red shields and jade axes, capped for the “Great Xia” suite.

sentences.zh: 」此之謂也。

translations.literal: ”This is what is meant.
translations.idiomatic: The passage refers to this very headdress.

sentences.zh: 通天冠，高九寸，正豎，頂少邪卻，乃直下爲鐵卷梁，前有山，展筩爲述，乘輿所常服。

translations.literal: The tongtianguan is nine inches high, set straight, the top slightly slanting backward, then running straight down with an iron curled beam; there is a “mountain” in front, and a spreading tube forms the “narrative”; it is what the imperial equipage ordinarily wears.
translations.idiomatic: The “pierce-heaven” crown rose nine inches, perfectly upright with a slight backward tilt, an iron roll forming the brim, a embossed “mountain” in front, and a horizontal tube—this was the emperor’s everyday court cap.

sentences.zh: 服衣，深衣制，有袍，隨五時色。

translations.literal: The garment is of deep-robe cut, with a robe, following the colors of the five seasons.
translations.idiomatic: He paired it with a deep-layered robe—effectively a gown—whose color shifted with the ritual season.

sentences.zh: 袍者，或曰周公抱成王宴居，故施袍。

translations.literal: As for the robe, some say the Duke of Zhou, embracing King Cheng in private leisure, therefore applied the robe.
translations.idiomatic: Commentators link the robe to the Duke of Zhou cradling the boy king at ease—hence the loose outer robe.

sentences.zh: 《禮記》「孔子衣逢掖之衣。

translations.literal: The Record of Rites: “Confucius wore the broad-sleeved garment.”
translations.idiomatic: The Book of Rites notes that Confucius favored wide-sleeved informal dress.

sentences.zh: 」縫掖其袖，合而縫大之，近今袍者也。

translations.literal: ”He stitched the sleeves at the armpit, joining and enlarging them; it is close to the robes of today.
translations.idiomatic: Those sleeves were pieced and widened under the arms—much like the modern administrative robe.

sentences.zh: 今下至賤更小吏，皆通制袍，單衣，皁緣領袖中衣，爲朝服云。

translations.literal: Down to petty clerks and the lowest minor officials, all universally make the robe, single garment, black-bordered collar and cuffs, and inner garment, as court dress, it is said.
translations.idiomatic: By Later Han even junior clerks wore a standardized robe and inner shirt with black facings as everyday court dress.

sentences.zh: 遠遊冠，制如通天，有展筩橫之於前，無山述，諸王所服也。

translations.literal: The yuanyouguan is patterned like the tongtianguan, with a spreading tube laid crosswise in front, but without mountain or “narrative”; it is what the kings wear.
translations.idiomatic: Princes wore the “far-roaming” crown—like the imperial cap but with a transverse tube in front and without the mountain-and-tube insignia of the Son of Heaven.

sentences.zh: 高山冠，一曰側注。

translations.literal: The gaoshanguan, one name is side-pour.
translations.idiomatic: The high-mountain cap was also called the “side-pour” crown.

sentences.zh: 制如通天，頂不邪卻，直豎，無山述展筩，中外官、謁者、僕射所服。

translations.literal: It is patterned like the tongtianguan, but the top does not slant backward, stands straight, and lacks mountain, narrative, or spreading tube; inner and outer officials and ushers and directors wear it.
translations.idiomatic: Shaped like the imperial cap but perfectly vertical, without the mountain motif or side tubes, it marked ushers, directors, and many civil officials.

sentences.zh: 太傅胡廣說曰：「高山冠，蓋齊王冠也。

translations.literal: Grand Tutor Hu Guang explained: “The gaoshanguan was probably the cap of the king of Qi.
translations.idiomatic: Hu Guang argued that this crown originated as the royal headgear of Qi.

sentences.zh: 秦滅齊，以其君冠賜近臣謁者服之。」

translations.literal: When Qin destroyed Qi, it gave the ruler’s cap to attendants and ushers to wear.”
translations.idiomatic: After Qin conquered Qi, the conquerors handed that royal cap down to palace ushers.

sentences.zh: 進賢冠，古緇布冠也，文儒者之服也。

translations.literal: The jinxianguan is the ancient black cloth cap; it is the dress of literati.
translations.idiomatic: The “advance-the-worthy” cap evolved from the ancient black cloth crown and identified scholars.

sentences.zh: 前高七寸，後高三寸，長八寸。

translations.literal: Seven inches high in front, three inches high in the rear, eight inches long.
translations.idiomatic: It measured seven inches in front, three in back, and eight along the brim.

sentences.zh: 公侯三梁，中二千石以下至博士兩梁，自博士以下至小史私學弟子，皆一梁。

translations.literal: Dukes and marquises have three ridges; from ministers at two thousand piculs down to erudits two ridges; from erudits downward to petty clerks and students of private schools, all have one ridge.
translations.idiomatic: The number of raised ribs signaled rank—three for the highest nobles, two for senior salary officials and academicians, one for everyone below.

sentences.zh: 宗室劉氏亦兩梁冠，示加服也。

translations.literal: Imperial clansmen of the Liu surname also wear the two-ridge cap, showing added dress.
translations.idiomatic: Even imperial kinsmen wore the two-ridged cap as a mark of honorific distinction.

sentences.zh: 法冠，一曰柱後。

translations.literal: The faguan, one name is pillar-behind.
translations.idiomatic: The law cap, also called “behind-the-pillar,” identified judicial officers.

sentences.zh: 高五寸，以纚爲展筩，鐵柱卷，執法者服之，侍御史，廷尉正監平也。

translations.literal: Five inches high, with gauze for the spreading tube, iron pillar curl; those who uphold the law wear it—attending censors, and the director, supervisors, and assistants of the commandant of justice.
translations.idiomatic: This stiff five-inch cap with iron upright and mesh “tube” was worn by censors and the senior staff of the Ministry of Justice.

sentences.zh: 或謂之獬豸冠。

translations.literal: Some call it the xiezhi cap.
translations.idiomatic: Popular speech called it the “unicorn-goat” law cap.

sentences.zh: 獬豸神羊，能別曲直，楚王嘗獲之，故以爲冠。

translations.literal: The xiezhi is a divine ram that can distinguish crooked from straight; the king of Chu once obtained one, and therefore made it a cap.
translations.idiomatic: Legend made the xiezhi a one-horned creature that knew justice from injustice; Chu’s kings turned its image into headgear.

sentences.zh: 胡廣說曰：「《春秋左氏傳》有南冠而縶者，則楚冠也。

translations.literal: Hu Guang explained: “The Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals speaks of a man in southern cap bound captive—then it is a Chu cap.
translations.idiomatic: Hu Guang cited the Zuo tradition: a prisoner in a “southern cap” meant the distinctive Chu court crown.

sentences.zh: 秦滅楚，以其君服賜執法近臣御史服之。」

translations.literal: When Qin destroyed Chu, it gave the ruler’s dress to attending officials and censors to wear.”
translations.idiomatic: Qin’s annexation of Chu left that royal cap to Han censors and close attendants.

sentences.zh: 武冠，一曰武弁大冠，諸武官冠之。

translations.literal: The wuguan, one name is great martial bian; various military officials cap with it.
translations.idiomatic: The great martial cap was the standard headgear of military officers.

sentences.zh: 侍中、中常侍加黃金璫，附蟬爲文，貂尾爲飾，謂之「趙惠文冠」。

translations.literal: Palace attendants and regular palace attendants add a gold knob, cicada pattern in front, and sable tail as ornament; it is called the “Marquis Huiwen cap.”
translations.idiomatic: Palace attendants gilded the cap with a front cicada plaque and sable tail—hence the nickname “Marquis Huiwen crown.”

sentences.zh: 胡廣說曰：「趙武靈王效胡服，以金璫飾首，前插貂尾，爲貴職。

translations.literal: Hu Guang explained: “King Wuling of Zhao copied Hu dress, using a gold knob to ornament the head, sable tails inserted in front, for exalted offices.
translations.idiomatic: Hu Guang recalled how King Wuling of Zhao adopted steppe fashions—gold knobs and sable plumes—for his highest ministers.

sentences.zh: 秦滅趙，以其君冠賜近臣。

translations.literal: When Qin destroyed Zhao, it gave the ruler’s cap to close attendants.
translations.idiomatic: After Qin swallowed Zhao, that princely cap passed to inner-court favorites.

sentences.zh: 」建武時，匈奴內屬，世祖賜南單於衣服，以中常侍惠文冠，中黃門童子佩刀云。

translations.literal: ”In the Jianwu era, when the Xiongnu submitted, the Founding Emperor granted the Southern Chanyu clothing, with the attendant’s Huiwen cap and yellow-gate lads with girdle swords, it is said.
translations.idiomatic: When the Southern Chanyu came in during Jianwu, Guangwu presented him with court dress that included the golden cicada cap and yellow-gate boys with ritual swords.

sentences.zh: 建華冠，以鐵爲柱卷，貫大銅珠九枚，制以縷鹿。

translations.literal: The jianhuaguan uses iron for the curled pillar, runs through nine great bronze beads, and is patterned with twisted deer.
translations.idiomatic: The “splendid bloom” crown stacked nine large bronze beads on an iron scroll frame in a deer-antler pattern.

sentences.zh: 記曰：「知天者冠述，知地者履絇。

translations.literal: The record says: “Those who know Heaven cap with the narrative; those who know Earth shoe with braided trim.”
translations.idiomatic: A gloss states: heaven-knowers wear the “narrative” tube; earth-knowers wear ridged shoes.

sentences.zh: 」《春秋左傳》曰：「鄭子臧好鷸冠。

translations.literal: ”The Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals says: “Zi Zang of Zheng loved the kingfisher cap.”
translations.idiomatic: The Zuo text mentions Zheng’s Zi Zang and his fondness for the kingfisher-feather crown.

sentences.zh: 」前圓，以爲此則是也。

translations.literal: ”Round in front; taking this as that, then this is correct.
translations.idiomatic: Its rounded front matches that description.

sentences.zh: 天地、五郊、明堂，《育命舞》樂人服之。

translations.literal: For Heaven and Earth, the five suburbs, and the Bright Hall, the musicians of the “Nurturing the Mandate” dance wear it.
translations.idiomatic: Dancers in the “Nurturing the Mandate” pageant wore it for cosmic and suburban rites.

sentences.zh: 方山冠，似進賢，以五采縠爲之。

translations.literal: The fangshanguan resembles the jinxianguan, made of five-colored thin silk.
translations.idiomatic: The square-mountain cap looked like the scholar’s cap but was built from iridescent thin gauze.

sentences.zh: 祠宗廟《大予》、《八佾》、《四時》、《五行》樂人服之，冠衣各如其行方之色而舞焉。

translations.literal: For ancestral temple sacrifice the musicians of the “Great Yu,” “Eight Rows,” “Four Seasons,” and “Five Phases” wear it; cap and robe each follow the color of the direction danced.
translations.idiomatic: Temple musicians in the major choreographed suites wore caps and coats dyed to the color of the cosmic direction they represented.

sentences.zh: 巧士冠，前高七寸，要後相通，直豎。

translations.literal: The qiaoshiguan is seven inches high in front, the waist and rear communicating, standing straight.
translations.idiomatic: The “ingenious gentleman” crown rose seven inches in front, with an open band running straight over the crown.

sentences.zh: 不常服，唯郊天，黃門從官四人冠之，在鹵簿中，次乘輿車前，以備宦者四星云。

translations.literal: It is not ordinarily worn; only at suburban sacrifice to Heaven do four yellow-gate attendants cap with it, in the escort, next in front of the imperial carriage, to supply the four stars of the eunuch asterism, it is said.
translations.idiomatic: Four eunuch attendants alone wore it at the suburban Heaven sacrifice, marching just ahead of the imperial chariot as stand-ins for the “four stars” of their constellation.

sentences.zh: 卻非冠，制似長冠，下促。

translations.literal: The quefeiguan is patterned like the changguan but shorter below.
translations.idiomatic: The “repel-wrong” cap copied the long cap but with a tighter, shorter skirt.

sentences.zh: 宮殿門吏僕射冠之。

translations.literal: Gatekeepers of palace halls and ushers cap with it.
translations.idiomatic: Palace gatekeepers and lead ushers wore it.

sentences.zh: 負赤幡，青翅燕尾，諸僕射幡皆如之。

translations.literal: They carry red banners with blue swallow-tails; all usher banners are like this.
translations.idiomatic: They shouldered crimson flags with blue swallow-tailed streamers—the standard usher banner.

sentences.zh: 卻敵冠，前高四寸，通長四寸，後高三寸，制似進賢，衛士服之。

translations.literal: The quediguan is four inches high in front, four inches through in total length, three inches high in back, patterned like the jinxianguan; guards wear it.
translations.idiomatic: The “repel-enemy” crown—four inches high fore and aft, three at the rear, cut like a scholar’s cap—went to the palace guard corps.

sentences.zh: 樊噲冠，漢將樊噲造次所冠，以入項羽軍。

translations.literal: The Fan Kuai cap is what Han general Fan Kuai caps in haste to enter Xiang Yu’s camp.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Kuai’s famous rush into Xiang Yu’s camp gave this emergency military cap its name.

sentences.zh: 廣九寸，高七寸，前後出各四寸，制似冕。

translations.literal: Nine inches wide, seven inches high, four inches protruding front and rear, patterned like a mianguan.
translations.idiomatic: It was nine inches broad, seven tall, with four-inch brims front and back like a miniature state crown.

sentences.zh: 司馬殿門大難，衛士服之。

translations.literal: At the great crisis at the Sima Gate, guards wear it.
translations.idiomatic: Guards donned it during the Sima Gate emergency.

sentences.zh: 或曰，樊噲常持鐵楯，聞項羽有意殺漢王，噲裂裳以裹楯，冠之入軍門，立漢王旁，視項羽。

translations.literal: Some say Fan Kuai always held an iron shield; hearing that Xiang Yu intended to kill the King of Han, Kuai tore his skirt to wrap the shield, capped himself, entered the camp gate, and stood beside the King of Han, staring at Xiang Yu.
translations.idiomatic: Tradition adds that Fan Kuai wrapped his shield in a torn skirt, jammed on this cap, burst through the gate, and glared at Xiang Yu from Liu Bang’s side.

sentences.zh: 術氏冠，前圓，吳制，差池邐迤四重，趙武靈王好服之。

translations.literal: The Shi clan cap is round in front, a Wu style, rippling in four layers; King Wuling of Zhao loved to wear it.
translations.idiomatic: The Shi-style round Wu cap, tiered in four rippling layers, was a favorite of King Wuling of Zhao.

sentences.zh: 今不施用，官有其圖注。

translations.literal: Today it is not applied; the offices have its diagram and commentary.
translations.idiomatic: Later courts retired it, though the archives still preserved its illustrated regulations.

sentences.zh: 諸冠皆有纓蕤，執事及武吏皆縮纓，垂五寸。

translations.literal: All caps have tassels and drooping threads; those who carry out duties and military clerks all shorten the tassel, hanging five inches.
translations.idiomatic: Every crown had cord tassels, but working officers and soldiers hitched them short—about five inches of hang.

sentences.zh: 武冠，俗謂之大冠，環纓無蕤，以青系爲緄，加雙鶡尾，豎左右，爲鶡冠云。

translations.literal: The wuguan, vulgarly called the great cap, has a ring tassel without drooping threads, with green cord for the border, adding paired pheasant tails, set vertically left and right, and it is called the heguan, it is said.
translations.idiomatic: The field version—popularly the “great cap”—used a ring knot, green edging, and twin pheasant plumes bolt upright: the true “pheasant cap.”

sentences.zh: 五官、左右虎賁、羽林、五中郎將、羽林左右監皆冠鶡冠，紗縠單衣。

translations.literal: The five household officers, left and right tiger brave, feather forest, five commandants of the gentles, and left and right supervisors of the feather forest all cap the heguan, with gauze single garment.
translations.idiomatic: Household guards, tiger braves, feather-forest archers, and related colonels all wore this pheasant cap with thin gauze tunics.

sentences.zh: 虎賁將虎文褲，白虎文劍佩刀。

translations.literal: Tiger brave officers wear tiger-pattern trousers and white tiger-pattern sword and girdle knife.
translations.idiomatic: Elite tiger brave units paired the cap with striped breeches and white-tiger motif blades.

sentences.zh: 虎賁武騎鶡冠，虎文單衣。

translations.literal: Tiger brave mounted archers heguan, tiger-pattern single garment.
translations.idiomatic: Mounted tiger braves wore the same crown with tiger-striped surcoats.

sentences.zh: 襄邑歲獻織成虎文云。

translations.literal: Xiangyi each year presents woven tiger patterns, it is said.
translations.idiomatic: Xiangyi county reportedly sent up loom-woven tiger designs each year.

sentences.zh: 鶡者，勇雉也，其鬥對一死乃止，故趙武靈王以表武士，秦施之焉。

translations.literal: The he is a courageous pheasant; in combat they face each other until one dies; therefore King Wuling of Zhao displayed warriors with it, and Qin applied it.
translations.idiomatic: The fighting cock-pheasant dies rather than yield, so Zhao’s martial king and later Qin used its plumes to brand elite troops.

sentences.zh: 安帝立皇太子，太子謁高祖廟、世祖廟，門大夫從，冠兩梁進貢；

translations.literal: When Emperor An established the heir apparent, the heir visited the shrines to Gaozu and the Founding Emperor; gate grandees followed, capped with the two-ridge jinxianguan;
translations.idiomatic: When Emperor An named a crown prince, the prince’s visits to the shrines of Gaozu and Guangwu were escorted by gate stewards in the two-ridged advance-the-worthy cap.

sentences.zh: 洗馬冠高山。

translations.literal: The groom of the heir apparent caps with the gaoshanguan.
translations.idiomatic: The heir apparent’s groom of the stable wore the high-mountain crown.

sentences.zh: 罷廟，侍御史任方奏請非乘從時，皆冠一梁，不宜以爲常服。

translations.literal: When the temple visit ended, Attending Censor Ren Fang submitted a memorial asking that, except when riding in attendance, all should cap with one ridge, and that it was not suitable to take this as ordinary dress.
translations.idiomatic: After the imperial shrines closed, Censor Ren Fang urged that the single-ridged cap be reserved for processional duty and not treated as everyday wear.

sentences.zh: 事下有司。

translations.literal: The matter was sent down to the responsible offices.
translations.idiomatic: The throne referred the proposal to the ministries for review.

sentences.zh: 尚書陳忠奏：「門大夫職如諫大夫，洗馬職如謁者，故皆服其服，先帝之舊也。

translations.literal: Director Chen Zhong submitted: “The gate grandee’s duties are like those of a remonstrance grandee, and the groom’s are like those of an usher; therefore each wears that office’s dress—this was the former emperors’ old rule.
translations.idiomatic: Chen Zhong replied that gate stewards ranked with remonstrance officials and grooms with ushers, so each should keep its prescribed headgear as under previous reigns.

sentences.zh: 方言可寢。

translations.literal: Ren Fang’s words may be shelved.
translations.idiomatic: Chen Zhong urged the throne to set aside Attendant Censor Ren Fang’s proposal.

sentences.zh: 」奏可。

translations.literal: ”The memorial was approved.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor endorsed that view.

sentences.zh: 謁者，古者一名洗馬。

translations.literal: The usher, in antiquity, had another name: groom of the stable.
translations.idiomatic: The text adds that “usher” was once simply another term for groom.

sentences.zh: 古者有冠無幘，其戴也，加首有頍，所以安物。

translations.literal: In antiquity there were caps but no ze kerchiefs; in wearing them, they added a kui band on the crown, by which to secure the ornaments.
translations.idiomatic: Early ritual dress used caps alone, without the wrapped kerchief; wearers steadied regalia with a forehead band before the ze evolved.

sentences.zh: 故《詩》曰：「有頍者弁」，此之謂也。

translations.literal: Therefore the Odes says: “How fine is he in his capped kui,” meaning this.
translations.idiomatic: The Book of Odes praises the capped youth with hanging kui—exactly this arrangement.

sentences.zh: 三代之世，法制滋彰，下至戰國，文武並用。

translations.literal: In the age of the Three Dynasties, laws and models grew ever clearer; down to the Warring States, civil and military usages were employed together.
translations.idiomatic: As the three ancient dynasties refined their codes, and even into the Warring States era, court dress served both civil and martial display.

sentences.zh: 秦雄諸侯，乃加其武將首飾爲絳袙，以表貴賤，其後稍稍作顏題。

translations.literal: Qin dominated the feudal lords, and therefore added to its generals’ headgear crimson wraps to mark noble and base; afterward they gradually fashioned forehead tablets.
translations.idiomatic: The Qin state distinguished its generals with crimson head-wraps to signal rank, then refined the look with stiffened forehead panels.

sentences.zh: 漢興，續其顏，卻摞之，施巾連題，卻覆之，今喪幘是其制也。

translations.literal: When Han arose, it continued the forehead tablet, drew the wrap back in folds, applied the kerchief joined to the tablet, and folded it back over—the mourning ze of today follow this construction.
translations.idiomatic: The Han kept the tablet, layered the cloth back from the brow, and linked kerchief to band in the shape still seen on mourning ze.

sentences.zh: 名之曰幘。

translations.literal: It was named the ze.
translations.idiomatic: That wrapped headcloth took the name ze.

sentences.zh: 幘者，賾也，頭首嚴賾也。

translations.literal: Ze means “packed”; the crown of the head is tightly packed.
translations.idiomatic: Etymologists gloss ze as “dense binding” around the skull.

sentences.zh: 至孝文乃高顏題，續之爲耳，崇其巾爲屋，合後施收，上下群臣貴賤皆服之。

translations.literal: Down to Emperor Xiaowen they raised the forehead tablet, extended it into ears, built the kerchief into a roof, joined the rear and applied a drawstring; high and low among the hundred officials all wore it.
translations.idiomatic: By Emperor Wen’s time the ze had acquired a tall front panel, side “ears,” a domed crown, and rear ties—universal from palaces to yamen.

sentences.zh: 文者長耳，武者短耳，稱其冠也。

translations.literal: Civil officials have long ears, martial short ears, matching their caps.
translations.idiomatic: Civil servants wore longer side tabs on the ze, soldiers shorter ones, keyed to their headgear.

sentences.zh: 尚書幘收，方三寸，名曰納言，示以忠正，顯近職也。

translations.literal: The Masters of Writing ze has a rear drawstring, three inches square, called “receiver of words,” to show loyalty and uprightness, displaying proximity to office.
translations.idiomatic: Secretariat officials sported a square rear flap called the “word-receiver,” advertising integrity and closeness to the throne.

sentences.zh: 迎氣五郊，各如其色，從章服也。

translations.literal: For welcoming the qi at the five suburbs, each follows its color, matching the emblem robe.
translations.idiomatic: At the five seasonal suburban rites, kerchief colors matched the directional vestments.

sentences.zh: 皁衣群吏春服青幘，立夏乃止，助微順氣，尊其方也。

translations.literal: Black-robed clerks in spring wear blue-green ze, until the Beginning of Summer, assisting the subtle qi and honoring that direction.
translations.idiomatic: Junior clerks in black robes donned green ze through spring to “help” the eastern qi, doffing them at summer’s start.

sentences.zh: 武吏常赤幘，成其威也。

translations.literal: Martial clerks constantly wear red ze, completing their awe.
translations.idiomatic: Military staff habitually wore crimson ze to heighten their formidable look.

sentences.zh: 未冠童子幘無屋者，示未成人也。

translations.literal: Boys not yet capped who wear ze without a roof show that they are not yet adult.
translations.idiomatic: Uncapped lads wore open-top ze to show they were still minors.

sentences.zh: 入學小童幘也句卷屋者，示尚幼少，未遠冒也。

translations.literal: School-entering children’s ze, those that also have a rolled roof, show that they are still very young and have not yet assumed full covering.
translations.idiomatic: Young boys beginning lessons wore ze with a small rolled crown, a sign that they were not yet grown enough for full adult headcloth.

sentences.zh: 喪幘卻摞反本，禮也，升數如冠，與冠偕也。

translations.literal: The mourning ze, drawn back in folds, returns to the root; it is ritual; the number of layers rises like the cap, together with the cap.
translations.idiomatic: Mourning ze folded backward echoed antiquity; their stacked layers paralleled those of mourning caps.

sentences.zh: 期喪起耳有收，素幘亦如之，禮輕重有制，變除從漸，文也。

translations.literal: One-year mourning raises the ears and has a drawstring; plain ze are likewise; ritual has light and heavy gradations, removal and change follow gradually—this is pattern.
translations.idiomatic: Even in reduced mourning, ze gained ear-tabs and ties; the code eased ornament step by step rather than all at once.

sentences.zh: 古者君臣佩玉，尊卑有度；

translations.literal: In antiquity lord and minister wore jade pendants, noble and base having their measures;
translations.idiomatic: Ancient courtiers all wore graded jade pendants to mark rank.

sentences.zh: 上有韨，貴賤有殊。

translations.literal: Above there was the fu kneepad, noble and base differing.
translations.idiomatic: The leather kneepad above the sash likewise differed by station.

sentences.zh: 佩，所以章德，服之衷也。

translations.literal: The pendant is that by which virtue is displayed; it is the inner of the dress.
translations.idiomatic: Pendants advertised moral standing—the inward truth of the costume.

sentences.zh: 韨，所以執事，禮之共也。

translations.literal: The fu is that by which one handles affairs; it is the shared ritual.
translations.idiomatic: The kneepad marked readiness for ritual service—shared ceremonial equipment.

sentences.zh: 故禮有其度，威儀之制，三代同之。

translations.literal: Therefore ritual has its measures; the system of awesome bearing, the Three Dynasties share it.
translations.idiomatic: Thus ornament and deportment stayed metered; the three dynasties held those rules in common.

sentences.zh: 五霸迭興，戰兵不息，佩非戰器，韨非兵旗，於是解去韨佩，留其係璲，以爲章表。

translations.literal: The Five Hegemons rose in turn, war weapons did not cease; pendants were not battle gear, fu not battle banners; therefore they untied fu and pendants, kept their linked sui, and used them as insignia.
translations.idiomatic: Endless warfare led hegemons to strip off heavy jade sets yet keep linked beads as badges of office.

sentences.zh: 故《詩》曰「鞙々佩璲」，此之謂也。

translations.literal: Therefore the Odes says “bright bright linked sui,” meaning this.
translations.idiomatic: The Odes’ “gleaming linked pendants” refer to this simplified regalia.

sentences.zh: 韨佩既廢，秦乃以採組連結於璲，光明章表，轉相結受，故謂之綬。

translations.literal: Once fu and pendants were abolished, Qin used colored cords linked to the sui, bright and manifest as insignia, turning and receiving one another; therefore it is called the shou ribbon.
translations.idiomatic: Qin replaced jade sets with bright silk cords knotted to seal-stones—origin of the named “ribbon” (shou).

sentences.zh: 漢承秦制，用而弗改，故加之以雙印佩刀之飾。

translations.literal: Han inherited Qin’s system, used it without change, and therefore added paired seals and girdle-knife ornament.
translations.idiomatic: Han kept Qin’s ribbons and layered on the double seal and court knife.

sentences.zh: 至孝明皇帝，乃爲大佩，衝牙雙瑀璜，皆以白玉。

translations.literal: Down to Emperor Xiaoming he made the great pendant, pounding-fang, paired yu, and huang, all of white jade.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Ming introduced the great court girdle—white jade pounding-teeth, paired disks, and huang plaques.

sentences.zh: 乘輿落以白珠，公卿諸侯以採絲，其玉視冕旒，爲祭服云。

translations.literal: The imperial equipage threads them with white pearls; dukes and ministers use colored silk; the jade matches the mianguan tassels, for sacrificial dress, it is said.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor’s set used pearl stringing; nobles used colored silk, with jade grades matching their crown tassels for sacrifice.

sentences.zh: 佩刀，乘輿黃金通身貂錯，半鮫魚鱗，金漆錯，雌黃室，五色罽隱室華。

translations.literal: The girdle knife: the imperial equipage is gold through the body with sable inlay, half shark-skin scales, gold lacquer inlay, orpiment chamber, five-colored felt hidden chamber splendor.
translations.idiomatic: The imperial dress knife was gold-inlaid with sable and sharkskin panels, lacquered fittings, and polychrome felt linings.

sentences.zh: 諸侯王黃金錯，環挾半鮫，黑室。

translations.literal: Feudal kings have gold inlay, ring-grip half shark, black chamber.
translations.idiomatic: Kings of blood carried gold-inlaid hilts with ring mounts and black scabbard chambers.

sentences.zh: 公卿百官皆純黑，不半鮫。

translations.literal: Dukes, ministers, and the hundred officials are all pure black, without half shark.
translations.idiomatic: Civil officials’ knives were plain black scabbards without the sharkskin half-panel.

sentences.zh: 小黃門雌黃室，中黃門朱室，童子皆虎爪文，虎賁黃室虎文，其將白虎文，皆以白珠鮫爲钅剽口之飾。

translations.literal: Junior yellow-gate has orpiment chamber, middle yellow-gate vermilion chamber; lads all have tiger-claw pattern; tiger brave yellow chamber tiger pattern; their generals white tiger pattern; all use white pearl shark for the mouth ornament.
translations.idiomatic: Eunuch ranks color-coded scabbard “chambers”; tiger guards bore tiger motifs; all used pearl and sharkskin at the throat of the sheath.

sentences.zh: 乘輿者，加翡翠山，紆嬰其側。

translations.literal: For the imperial equipage, add a jadeite mountain, with twisted tassels at its side.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor alone added a jadeite mountain mount with hanging tassels on the blade.

sentences.zh: 佩雙印，長寸二分，方六分。

translations.literal: The paired seals hang at one inch two tenths long, six tenths square.
translations.idiomatic: Double ritual seals measured about 1.2 inches long and 0.6 inch square.

sentences.zh: 乘輿、諸侯王、公、列侯以白玉，中二千石以下至四百石皆以黑犀，二百石以至私學弟子皆以像牙。

translations.literal: The imperial equipage, feudal kings, dukes, and ranked marquises use white jade; from ministers at two thousand piculs down to four hundred piculs all use black rhinoceros; from two hundred piculs down to private-school students all use ivory.
translations.idiomatic: Seal material followed rank—white jade for the throne and top nobility, black horn for mid officials, ivory for humbler clerks and students.

sentences.zh: 上合絲，乘輿以縢貫白珠，赤罽蕤，諸侯王以下以綔赤絲蕤，縢綔各如其印質。

translations.literal: The upper is joined with silk; the imperial equipage threads it with white pearls and red felt tassels; feudal kings downward use mixed red silk tassels; the cord colors match each seal’s substance.
translations.idiomatic: Imperial cords carried white pearls and crimson tassels; lower ranks used blended red silk keyed to the seal stone.

sentences.zh: 刻書文曰：「正月剛卯既決，靈殳四方，赤青白黃，四色是當。

translations.literal: The engraved text says: “In the first month the gang-mao is already fixed; the spirit staff to the four directions, red, green, white, yellow—the four colors are correct.
translations.idiomatic: The spring amulet’s incantation invokes the gang-mao charm’s power over the four quarters in their proper colors.

sentences.zh: 帝令祝融，以教夔龍，庶疫剛癉，莫我敢當。

translations.literal: The emperor orders Zhurong to instruct the kui dragons; may pestilence and hard illness not dare withstand us.”
translations.idiomatic: It calls on the fire god Zhurong and dragon spirits to ward off plague—no demon may resist.

sentences.zh: 疾日嚴卯，帝令夔化，慎爾週伏，化茲靈殳。

translations.literal: “On the yan-mao day of affliction, the emperor orders Kui to transform; be careful in your hiding; transform this spirit staff.
translations.idiomatic: The summer yan-mao face adds lines commanding the spirit Kui to transform hidden banes.

sentences.zh: 既正既直，既觚既方，庶疫剛癉，莫我敢當。

translations.literal: Already straight already upright, already angular already square; may pestilence and hard illness not dare withstand us.”
translations.idiomatic: It ends by declaring the charm square and true so that illness cannot prevail.

sentences.zh: 」凡六十六字。

translations.literal: ”In all sixty-six characters.
translations.idiomatic: The full inscription ran to sixty-six graphs.

sentences.zh: 乘輿黃赤綬，四採，黃赤縹紺，淳黃圭，長二丈九尺九寸，五百首。

translations.literal: The imperial equipage yellow-red shou, four hues—yellow, red, light green, and dark blue—pure yellow gui, two zhang nine chi nine cun long, five hundred strands.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor’s ribbon mixed four colors on a pure yellow boss, nearly three yards long with five hundred woven “heads.”

sentences.zh: 諸侯王赤綬，四採，赤黃縹紺，淳赤圭，長二丈一尺，三百首。

translations.literal: Feudal kings have red shou, four hues—red, yellow, light green, dark blue—pure red gui, two zhang one chi long, three hundred strands.
translations.idiomatic: Kings of Liu blood wore a red-based four-color ribbon about twenty-one feet long.

sentences.zh: 太皇太后、皇太后，其綬皆與乘輿同，皇后亦如之。

translations.literal: The Grand Empress Dowager and Empress Dowager have shou identical to the imperial equipage; the empress is likewise.
translations.idiomatic: The two dowagers and the reigning empress used the same ribbon scheme as the emperor.

sentences.zh: 長公主、天子貴人與諸侯王同綬者，加特也。

translations.literal: The senior princess and the Son of Heaven’s noble consorts who share feudal kings’ shou receive special advancement.
translations.idiomatic: Senior princesses and top imperial ladies who matched princely ribbons did so by special favor.

sentences.zh: 諸國貴人、相國皆綠綬，三采，綠紫紺，淳綠圭，長二丈一尺，二百四十首。

translations.literal: Nobles of the various states and chancellors all have green shou, three hues—green, purple, dark blue—pure green gui, two zhang one chi long, two hundred forty strands.
translations.idiomatic: Kingdom nobles and chancellors wore triple-hued green ribbons about twenty-one feet long.

sentences.zh: 公、侯、將軍紫綬，二採，紫白、淳紫圭，長丈七尺，百八十首。

translations.literal: Dukes, marquises, and generals have purple shou, two hues—purple and white—pure purple gui, one zhang seven chi long, one hundred eighty strands.
translations.idiomatic: Dukes, marquises, and generals bore purple-and-white ribbons seventeen feet long.

sentences.zh: 公主封君服紫綬。

translations.literal: Princesses and titled ladies wear purple shou.
translations.idiomatic: Ennobled princesses and dames wore the purple grade.

sentences.zh: 九卿、中二千石、二千石青綬，三采，青白紅，淳青圭，長丈七尺，百二十首。

translations.literal: The Nine Ministers, ministers at two thousand piculs, and two thousand piculs have blue-green shou, three hues—blue-green, white, red—pure blue-green gui, one zhang seven chi long, one hundred twenty strands.
translations.idiomatic: Ministry heads and salary-class two thousand piculs used a three-color blue-green ribbon seventeen feet long.

sentences.zh: 自青綬以上，縌皆長三尺二寸，與綬同採而首半之。

translations.literal: From blue-green shou upward, the secondary ribbon (ni) is three chi two cun long, same hues as the shou but half the strand count.
translations.idiomatic: Above that rank a shorter “ni” cord matched the main ribbon’s colors at half density.

sentences.zh: 縌者，古佩璲也。

translations.literal: The ni is the ancient linked sui.
translations.idiomatic: That secondary cord descended from the old jade-link strings.

sentences.zh: 佩綬相迎受，故曰縌。

translations.literal: Pendant and shou meet and receive each other; therefore it is called ni.
translations.idiomatic: Because it paired with the main shou, ritualists called it ni.

sentences.zh: 紫綬以上，縌綬之間得施玉環鐍云。

translations.literal: From purple shou upward, jade rings and metal slides may be set between ni and shou, it is said.
translations.idiomatic: Purple ranks and higher might add jade rings and metal slides between the two cords.

sentences.zh: 千石、六百石黑綬，三采，青赤紺，淳青圭，長丈六尺，八十首。

translations.literal: One thousand piculs and six hundred piculs have black shou, three hues—blue-green, red, dark blue—pure blue-green gui, one zhang six chi long, eighty strands.
translations.idiomatic: County-level salaries wore black-based triple hues sixteen feet long.

sentences.zh: 四百石、三百石長同。

translations.literal: Four hundred piculs and three hundred piculs share the same length.
translations.idiomatic: The four-hundred and three-hundred picul grades used identical ribbon lengths.

sentences.zh: 四百石、三百石、二百石黃綬，一採，淳黃圭，長丈五尺，六十首。

translations.literal: Four hundred piculs, three hundred piculs, and two hundred piculs have yellow shou, one hue—pure yellow gui, one zhang five chi long, sixty strands.
translations.idiomatic: Lower magistrates bore plain yellow ribbons fifteen feet long.

sentences.zh: 自黑綬以下，縌綬皆長三尺，與綬同採而首半之。

translations.literal: From black shou downward, ni and shou are each three chi long, same hues as the shou but half the strand count.
translations.idiomatic: Below black rank, both cords shortened to three feet while keeping the half-density rule.

sentences.zh: 百石青紺綬，一採，宛轉繆織圭，長丈二尺。

translations.literal: One hundred piculs have blue-dark shou, one hue, twisting wrongly woven gui, one zhang two chi long.
translations.idiomatic: The lowest salaried grade used a twelve-foot blue-black cord in twined weave.

sentences.zh: 凡先合單紡爲一系，四系爲一扶，五扶爲一首，五首成一文，文采淳爲一圭。

translations.literal: In general, first combine single spun threads into one cord, four cords make a fu, five fu make a tou, five tou make a pattern, pattern purity makes one gui.
translations.idiomatic: Weavers counted threads: four plies to a bundle, five bundles to a “head,” five heads to a pattern block forming one color boss.

sentences.zh: 首多者係細，少者係粗，皆廣尺六寸。

translations.literal: Many heads mean fine ties, few mean coarse ties; all are one chi six cun wide.
translations.idiomatic: Higher strand counts meant finer weave, yet every ribbon stayed the same width.

sentences.zh: 太皇太后、皇太后入廟服，紺上皁下，蠶，青上縹下，皆深衣制，隱領袖緣以絛。

translations.literal: Grand Empress Dowager and Empress Dowager temple dress: dark blue upper, black lower; for silkworm rites, green upper, light green lower—all deep-robe cut, hidden collar and cuffs bordered with tape.
translations.idiomatic: Dowagers entering the temple wore dark layered robes; for the silkworm ceremony they shifted to green tones, always deep-robe cut with tape-edged hidden collars.

sentences.zh: 剪氂蔮，簪珥。

translations.literal: Cut yak hair covering, hairpin and earrings.
translations.idiomatic: They added a yak-hair veil, hairpins, and ear pendants.

sentences.zh: 珥。

translations.literal: Earrings.
translations.idiomatic: Earrings.

sentences.zh: 耳璫垂珠也。

translations.literal: Ear dang with hanging pearls.
translations.idiomatic: “Ear dang” meant pearl drops at the lobe.

sentences.zh: 簪以玳瑁爲擿，長一尺，端爲華勝，上爲鳳皇爵，以翡翠爲毛羽，下有白珠，垂黃金鑷。

translations.literal: The hairpin uses tortoiseshell for the pin, one chi long, the end a floral sheng, above it a phoenix sparrow, with jadeite for feathers, below white pearls, hanging gold tweezers.
translations.idiomatic: Their hairpins were tortoiseshell shafts a foot long, topped with jeweled “floral crests,” phoenix finials of jadeite feathers, pearl strings, and gold picks.

sentences.zh: 左右一橫簪之，以安蔮結。

translations.literal: Left and right a horizontal hairpin secures it, to settle the covering’s knot.
translations.idiomatic: Cross-pins fixed the headdress and veil knot.

sentences.zh: 諸簪珥皆同制，其擿有等級焉。

translations.literal: All hairpins and earrings share one pattern, but the pins have grades.
translations.idiomatic: The same basic design scaled by rank in pin ornament.

sentences.zh: 皇后謁廟服，紺上皁下，蠶，青上縹下，皆深衣制，隱領袖緣以絛。

translations.literal: The empress’s temple dress: dark blue upper, black lower; for silkworm rites, green upper, light green lower—all deep-robe cut, hidden collar and cuffs bordered with tape.
translations.idiomatic: The empress mirrored the dowagers’ temple and silkworm palettes on deep robes with taped hidden collars.

sentences.zh: 假結。

translations.literal: False topknot.
translations.idiomatic: She wore a formal wig-knot.

sentences.zh: 步搖，簪珥。

translations.literal: Bu yao, hairpins and earrings.
translations.idiomatic: Her regalia included the swaying bu yao crown, pins, and earrings.

sentences.zh: 步搖以黃金爲山題，貫白珠爲桂枝相繆，一爵九華，熊、虎、赤羆、天鹿、辟邪、南山豐大特六獸，《詩》所謂「副笄六珈」者。

translations.literal: The bu yao uses gold for the mountain tablet, strung white pearls as cassia branches intertwining, one sparrow nine blooms, bear, tiger, red bear, celestial deer, bixie, Nanshan abundant great bull—the six beasts—what the Odes calls “side hairpins with six jia.”
translations.idiomatic: Her bu yao showed a gold “mountain,” pearl “cassia” sprays, nine blossoms to a finial, and six jeweled beasts—the Odes’ “six jia upon the side pins.”

sentences.zh: 諸爵獸皆以翡翠爲毛羽。

translations.literal: All sparrow beasts use jadeite for feathers.
translations.idiomatic: Every bird-and-beast finial used jadeite inlay for plumage.

sentences.zh: 金題，白珠璫繞，以翡翠爲華云。

translations.literal: Gold tablet, white pearl dang circling, with jadeite blossoms, it is said.
translations.idiomatic: Gold plaques, pearl circlets, and jadeite flowers completed the crown.

sentences.zh: 貴人助蠶服，純縹上下，深衣制。

translations.literal: Noble consorts assisting at silkworm rites: pure light green upper and lower, deep-robe cut.
translations.idiomatic: Imperial consorts of honor wore monochrome light green deep robes at the silkworm altar.

sentences.zh: 大手結，墨玳瑁，又加簪珥。

translations.literal: Large hand knot, ink tortoiseshell, again adding hairpins and earrings.
translations.idiomatic: They used a large hand-shaped coiffure, dark tortoiseshell pins, and full ear jewelry.

sentences.zh: 長公主見會衣服，加步搖，公主大手結，皆有簪珥，衣服同制。

translations.literal: The senior princess at court meetings adds bu yao; princesses use the large hand knot; all have hairpins and earrings; clothes share the same pattern.
translations.idiomatic: Senior princesses gained bu yao for audiences while lesser princesses kept the large knot; all shared pin-and-earring rules.

sentences.zh: 自公主封君以上皆帶綬，以採組爲緄帶，各如其綬色。

translations.literal: From princess and titled lady upward all wear shou, using colored cords for the border belt, each matching its shou color.
translations.idiomatic: Titled women from princess rank up wore ribbons with belt borders dyed to match.

sentences.zh: 黃金辟邪，首爲帶鐍，飾以白珠。

translations.literal: Gold bixie, head forming belt slide, ornamented with white pearls.
translations.idiomatic: Their belt slides were gold bixie beasts inset with pearls.

sentences.zh: 公、卿、列侯、中二千石、二千石夫人，紺繒蔮，黃金龍首銜白珠，魚須擿，長一尺，爲簪珥，入廟佐祭者皁絹上下，助蠶者縹絹上下，皆深衣制，緣。

translations.literal: Wives of dukes, ministers, ranked marquises, ministers at two thousand piculs, and two thousand piculs: dark silk covering, gold dragon head holding white pearls, fish-whisker pin one chi long, as hairpins and earrings; those entering the temple to assist sacrifice wear black silk upper and lower; those assisting silkworm light green silk upper and lower—all deep-robe cut, bordered.
translations.idiomatic: Elite wives wore dark veils, dragon-headed pearl pins, and fish-bone hairpins; temple duty meant black deep robes, silkworm duty pale green, all edged per code.

sentences.zh: 自二千石夫人以上至皇后，皆以蠶衣爲朝服。

translations.literal: From two thousand piculs’ wives upward to the empress, all take silkworm dress as court dress.
translations.idiomatic: From ministerial wives to the empress, the silkworm robe doubled as court dress.

sentences.zh: 公主、貴人、妃以上，嫁娶得服錦綺羅縠繒，採十二色，重緣袍。

translations.literal: Princesses, noble consorts, and consorts of rank and above, in marrying may wear brocade, damask, gauze, and silk, twelve colors of hues, heavy-bordered robes.
translations.idiomatic: High-ranking ladies could marry in twelve-hued brocades and multi-layered bordered gowns.

sentences.zh: 特進、列侯以上錦繒，採十二色。

translations.literal: Specially advanced and ranked marquises upward use brocade silk, twelve colors of hues.
translations.idiomatic: Specially advanced nobles and marquises enjoyed the full twelve-color brocade palette.

sentences.zh: 六百石以上重練，採九色，禁丹紫紺。

translations.literal: Six hundred piculs upward use heavy refined silk, nine colors of hues, forbidding cinnabar, purple, and dark blue.
translations.idiomatic: Six-hundred picul households could use nine hues but not the top three forbidden shades.

sentences.zh: 三百石以上五色採，青絳黃紅綠。

translations.literal: Three hundred piculs upward five colors of hues: blue-green, crimson, yellow, red, green.
translations.idiomatic: Three-hundred picul rank allowed a five-color set within those limits.

sentences.zh: 二百石以上四採，青黃紅綠。

translations.literal: Two hundred piculs upward four hues: blue-green, yellow, red, green.
translations.idiomatic: Two-hundred picul clerks were limited to four hues.

sentences.zh: 賈人，緗縹而已。

translations.literal: Merchants, light yellow and light green only.
translations.idiomatic: Merchants could wear only pale yellow and pale green.

sentences.zh: 公、列侯以下皆單緣襈，製文繡爲祭服，自皇后以下，皆不得服諸古麗圭襂閨緣加上之服。

translations.literal: Dukes and ranked marquises downward all have single-border lined jackets; regulated brocade becomes sacrificial dress; from the empress downward, none may wear various ancient gorgeous gui-overlays, boudoir borders, or added-on upper garments.
translations.idiomatic: High nobles wore single-border coats; regulated brocade served sacrifice; from the empress down, archaic layered finery and private-chamber trims were banned.

sentences.zh: 建武、永平禁絕之，建初、永元又復中重，於是世莫能有製其裁者，乃遂絕矣。

translations.literal: Jianwu and Yongping utterly forbade them; Jianchu and Yongyuan again restored middle-heavy layers; then none in the age could regulate the cutting, and so they were finally cut off.
translations.idiomatic: Early Eastern Han bans collapsed under later reigns’ fashion excess until tailors could no longer police the cuts and the court abandoned the fight.

sentences.zh: 凡冠衣諸服，旒冕、長冠、委貌、皮弁、爵弁、建華、方山、巧士，衣裳文繡，赤舄，服絇履，大佩，皆爲祭服，其餘悉爲常用朝服。

translations.literal: In general for caps and robes of all dress, mianguan, changguan, weimao, pibian, juebian, jianhua, fangshan, qiaoshi, patterned robe and skirt, red shoes, braided shoes, great pendant—all are sacrificial dress; the rest are all ordinary court dress.
translations.idiomatic: The listed crowns, brocade robes, red shoes, great jade girdle, and braided shoes counted as sacrifice-only; everything else was routine court wear.

sentences.zh: 唯長冠，諸王國謁者以爲常朝服云。

translations.literal: Only the changguan—feudal kingdom ushers take it as ordinary court dress, it is said.
translations.idiomatic: Only the long cap, among princely households’ ushers, doubled as everyday dress.

sentences.zh: 宗廟以下，祠祀皆冠長冠，皁繒袍單衣，絳緣領袖中衣，絳褲襪，五郊各從其色焉。

translations.literal: Below the ancestral temple, for all cult sacrifice they cap changguan, black silk robe and single garment, crimson-bordered collar and cuffs on inner dress, crimson trousers and socks; the five suburbs each follow their color.
translations.idiomatic: For lesser shrines and cult sites, officers wore the long cap with black robe, crimson-trimmed underlayers, and directional colors at the five suburban altars.

sentences.zh: 贊曰：車輅各庸，旌旂異局。

translations.literal: The eulogy says: Carriages each have their function; banners and flags differ in arrangement.
translations.idiomatic: The historian’s verse praises how chariots suit their tasks and how each banner keeps its station.

sentences.zh: 冠服緻美，佩紛璽玉。

translations.literal: Caps and robes are finely wrought; pendants array seals and jade.
translations.idiomatic: Crown and robe reach exquisite polish; girdle ornaments set off jade and seals.

sentences.zh: 敬敬報情，尊尊下欲。

translations.literal: With reverent care they respond to circumstance; honoring the honored, they place desire below.
translations.idiomatic: Ritual answered the moment with grave care: rank was honored and private appetite kept in its place.

sentences.zh: 孰誇華文，匪豪麗縟。

translations.literal: Who would boast of splendid patterns? They are not mere luxury and rich excess.
translations.idiomatic: This was never vainglory in ornament—nothing here was swagger or empty sumptuousness.
